primary.title: Cryo-EM advances in TDP-43 amyloid fibrils structure determination.
primary.abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is a DNA/RNA-binding protein whose pathological aggregation characterizes a spectrum of neurodegenerative disorders known as TDP-43 proteinopathies, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Recent breakthroughs in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) have revolutionized our understanding of these diseases by resolving the atomic structures of TDP-43 amyloid fibrils. These structural insights have been pivotal in elucidating the transition from functional liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to irreversible solid-state aggregation. This review synthesizes key cryo-EM findings from 2019 to 2026, encompassing fibrils formed by the full-length low-complexity domain, disease-relevant core fragments, and filaments extracted directly from patient tissues, as well as the pathological implications of distinct structural polymorphs. These findings not only deepen our understanding of the brain science aspects of the pathogenesis of TDP-43 proteinopathies, but also provide an important structural basis for the development of specific conformational diagnostic methods and targeted therapeutic drugs.

primary.title: Pathological Priming and Developmental Heterochrony as Organizing Concepts in Human iPSC Models of Autism Spectrum Disorder.
primary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition in which diverse genetic risk factors converge on molecular pathways governing early brain development. Human-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) and brain organoid models now permit direct interrogation of these pathways in patient-derived neural tissue and, in a subset of studies, reveal alterations in neural progenitor proliferation, cortical neurogenesis, synaptic maturation, and network excitability. A landmark iPSC study in macrocephalic idiopathic ASD introduced the concept of pathological priming of neural progenitors, durable reconfiguration of chromatin and transcriptional states that biases downstream developmental programs, and associated developmental heterochrony in neuronal gene networks, thereby linking early progenitor biology to selectively shifted trajectories of neuronal maturation and to macrostructural and functional abnormalities. This conceptual review synthesizes evidence for pathological priming and developmental heterochrony from human iPSC-derived neurons and brain organoids, focusing on the ASD subgroups in which timing mechanisms are best supported: macrocephalic idiopathic ASD, 16p11.2 and related copy number variants, and large-effect developmental regulators such as SYNGAP1. We summarize recurrent and inconsistent cellular and circuit phenotypes, evaluate multi-omic data implicating progenitor regulatory states in shaping developmental timing, and situate timing-focused mechanisms alongside synaptopathy, excitatory-inhibitory imbalance, critical-period, and neuroimmune models. We propose that disturbances in neurodevelopmental timing characterize specific ASD subgroups, particularly those with early brain overgrowth or large-effect developmental regulators, rather than ASD as a whole, and offer a useful organizing principle for integrating divergent findings and generating testable, timing-informed hypotheses for future experimental and translational work.

primary.title: Restoring Neural Homeostasis via Class II HDAC Modulation: Mechanistic Insights and Therapeutic Opportunities.
primary.abstract: Class II histone deacetylases (HDACs) comprise class IIa enzymes HDAC4, HDAC5, HDAC7, and HDAC9 and class IIb enzymes HDAC6 and HDAC10, which differ substantially in structure, catalytic activity, subcellular localization, and neural function. Class IIa HDACs exhibit weak intrinsic deacetylase activity and function predominantly as signal-responsive scaffolds that couple calcium and kinase signaling to transcription through nucleocytoplasmic shuttling, recruitment of HDAC3-containing NCoR/SMRT corepressor complexes, and interactions with MEF2, CREB, and FOXO. Conversely, HDAC6 is a predominantly cytoplasmic deacetylase that regulates α-tubulin acetylation, cytoskeletal dynamics, axonal transport, autophagy, and proteostasis. Dysregulated class II HDAC signaling contributes to neurodegenerative diseases through convergent mechanisms involving synaptic dysfunction, maladaptive transcriptional repression, mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption, and defective clearance of pathological proteins. Disease-associated substrates include amyloid-β and tau in Alzheimer's disease, α-synuclein in Parkinson's disease, mutant huntingtin in Huntington's disease, and TDP-43/SOD1 in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Emerging evidence additionally links aberrant HDAC4/5 signaling to neurodevelopmental disorders through altered synaptic maturation, excitation-inhibition balance, and circuit development. This review integrates the structural and mechanistic biology of class II HDACs with their disease-specific roles and evaluates therapeutic approaches to restore neural homeostasis. Particular emphasis is placed on selective HDAC6 inhibitors, modulation of class IIa protein-protein interactions and subcellular trafficking, natural compounds, and RNA-based strategies. Finally, we discuss major translational challenges, including isoform specificity, brain penetration, context-dependent functions, and the need to distinguish catalytic from non-enzymic mechanisms when developing disease-modifying interventions for neurological disorders while preserving normal essential HDAC functions and minimizing off-target toxicity.

primary.title: Therapeutic Timing at Mitochondrial Redox-Autophagy-Mitophagy Checkpoints in Age-Related Hearing Loss.
primary.abstract: Age-related hearing loss (ARHL) is common, disabling, and still managed largely with compensatory devices rather than mechanism-modifying therapy. The major weakness in the current translational pipeline is not the absence of candidate pathways, but the lack of a timing framework that links cochlear phenotype, mitochondrial injury state, and intervention intensity. This revised Review therefore focuses on a staged mitochondrial redox-quality-control model. We argue that ARHL emerges when high-energy cochlear compartments-outer and inner hair cells, spiral ganglion neurons, and the lateral wall/stria vascularis-cross a threshold at which mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS), impaired mitochondrial DNA and transfer RNA integrity, lysosomal insufficiency, and incomplete mitophagy reinforce each other. Three checkpoints are emphasized because they are mechanistically actionable and experimentally measurable: NAD+-SIRT3-dependent mitochondrial deacetylation and antioxidant stabilization, NRF2-dependent redox and detoxification buffering, and PINK1-Parkin-dependent selective mitophagy. We also expand the sidewall perspective, highlighting that strial and spiral ligament redox instability can reduce endocochlear-potential reserve and modify the apparent sensory-neural phenotype. A practical therapeutic sequence is proposed: early substrate reinforcement through NAD+-SIRT3 and NRF2; mid-stage restoration of autophagy-lysosome competence; and selective mitophagy enhancement only when flux, not merely marker accumulation, is demonstrably limiting. Finally, we define a biomarker and detection framework that distinguishes cochlear tissue endpoints from blood or perilymph proxies and separates mouse proof-of-mechanism from human trial stratification. This approach clarifies which evidence is sufficient for prevention studies, which remains missing, and how future ARHL trials can be aligned with mechanism and timing.

primary.title: Wiring the developing brain: The Rho GTPase signaling network in neurodevelopmental disorders.
primary.abstract: Human genetics has substantially advanced our understanding of the Rho GTPase signaling network in brain development and established its dysregulation as an important mechanism underlying neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). Through the spatiotemporal control of actin cytoskeleton dynamics, canonical and atypical Rho GTPases, together with their guanine nucleotide exchange factors, GTPase-activating proteins, guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitors, and downstream effectors, regulate major stages of corticogenesis, including neural progenitor proliferation and polarity, neuronal migration, axonal and dendritic development, synapse formation, and circuit maturation. Recent genomic studies have expanded the spectrum of Rho GTPase-related disorders by identifying pathogenic variants in core pathway genes, including RAC1, RAC3, CDC42, RHOA, and RHOBTB2, as well as in regulators and pathway-associated genes such as TRIO, OPHN1, ARHGEF9, ARHGAP31, DENND5A, DENND5B, and AUTS2. These findings indicate that genetically heterogeneous conditions, including autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, developmental and epileptic encephalopathies, and structural brain abnormalities, converge on shared developmental processes governing cytoskeletal remodeling, neuronal morphogenesis, synaptic organization, and connectivity. In this Review, we integrate the molecular architecture of Rho GTPase signaling with its physiological roles throughout corticogenesis and link individual signaling modules and disease-associated genes to clinical phenotypes and experimentally validated pathogenic mechanisms. This framework highlights how disruption of distinct components of the Rho GTPase network produces overlapping neurodevelopmental phenotypes through perturbation of common cellular and developmental programs.

primary.title: The ferroptosis-neuroinflammation feedback loop in traumatic brain injury: mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
primary.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of death and disability worldwide, with secondary injury processes such as ferroptosis and neuroinflammation adding to its detrimental effects. Recent studies reveal a profound bidirectional interaction. On one hand, inflammation drives ferroptosis by disrupting iron homeostasis through the IL-6/Janus kinase 2 (JAK2)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3)-hepcidin axis, impairing the system Xc-/glutathione (GSH)/GPX4 antioxidant system and promoting immune cell infiltration. Conversely, ferroptotic cells release damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), including high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) and lipid peroxidation end-products like 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), which activate toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling and fuel a neuroinflammatory vicious cycle. We further discuss emerging therapeutic approaches targeting this axis, including ferroptosis inhibitors (Fer-1, Lip-1), dual-regulatory agents (annexin A5, melatonin, and H2S), and exosome-based delivery systems, while highlighting translational difficulties presented by the BBB and complex time windows. This review presents a framework to comprehend the interplay between ferroptosis and inflammation and to guide the development of dual-targeted treatments in TBI.

primary.title: Convergent molecular mechanisms of chronic heavy metal exposure and repetitive mild traumatic brain injury in neurodegenerative processes.
primary.abstract: Repetitive mild traumatic brain injury (rmTBI) and chronic environmental exposure to heavy metals represent widespread contributors to neurological dysfunction that are typically studied independently. However, emerging evidence indicates that these insults converge on overlapping cellular pathways that disrupt neuronal homeostasis, redox balance, genomic stability and proteostasis, including tau regulation. Notably, environmental metals including mercury, lead, arsenic, cadmium, and hexavalent chromium induce oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuroinflammatory signaling, processes that are also central to rmTBI pathophysiology. In this review, we synthesize mechanistic and clinical evidence linking chronic heavy metal exposure and rmTBI and examine how their interaction may influence long-term vulnerability to neurodegeneration. To our knowledge, this is the first review to integrate these two domains within a unified mechanistic framework. We first summarize shared and metal-specific mechanisms of heavy metal neurotoxicity and integrate these findings with the cellular and systemic consequences of rmTBI. Attention is given to higher-order convergent processes, including disruption of the blood-brain barrier, dysregulation of the gut-brain axis, protein misfolding and tau pathology, ferroptosis, and impairment of proteostatic and autophagic pathways. We also discuss emerging biomarker signatures and therapeutic targets relevant to combined environmental and traumatic exposures. Collectively, current evidence supports a model in which chronic heavy metal burden may diminish neural resilience and could increase vulnerability to the cumulative effects of rmTBI. Although direct evidence of their interaction remains limited, the substantial mechanistic overlap provides a framework for future studies investigating environmental contributions to post-traumatic neurodegeneration, biomarker discovery, and potential therapeutic strategies.

primary.title: The role of neurofilament light chain and other fluid biomarkers in cerebellar ataxias.
primary.abstract: The genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity of hereditary ataxias complicates the design of clinical trials since each ataxia progresses at different rates. Consequently, robust biomarkers are urgently needed to monitor therapeutic efficacy and safety of potential therapeutic interventions. Neurofilament light chain has emerged as a leading candidate, serving as a sensitive pharmacodynamic biomarker of neuronal injury and treatment response in neurodegenerative disorders. This review explores the utility of neurofilament light chain across various ataxias, including polyglutamine spinocerebellar ataxias, Friedreich's ataxia, multiple system atrophy, and other genetic ataxias, such as ataxias associated with RCF1 and SPG7 genes. We synthesize evidence from recent studies that have used ultra-sensitive assays. These studies consistently demonstrate elevated neurofilament light chain levels in cerebrospinal fluid and blood, correlating with disease severity, progression and neuroimaging findings. Notably, neurofilament light chain levels rise during the presymptomatic stage in spinocerebellar ataxias, highlighting its potential for stratifying individuals for trial enrolment and tracking therapeutic effects. A treatment-induced reduction in neurofilament light chain could function as a surrogate endpoint for target engagement, analogous to its validated use in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Finally, we discuss the results of other studies conducted on other biomarkers, including glial fibrillary acidic protein, total tau and phosphorylated tau, which may reflect complementary aspects of neurodegeneration and glial activation. Glial fibrillary acidic protein may provide insights into astroglial reactivity and neuroinflammation. Similarly, alteration in total tau and phosphorylated tau levels may suggest dysfunction in neuronal cytoskeleton and axonal integrity. The review also focuses on target-engagement biomarkers, including polyglutamine-expanded ataxin proteins in spinocerebellar ataxias and frataxin in Friedreich's ataxia, as critical tools to complement the ataxia biomarker toolkit. The quantification of mutant ataxin proteins provides a mechanistic readout for emerging gene-silencing or protein-lowering therapies. In parallel, the measurement of frataxin levels serves as a pharmacodynamic marker in therapeutic strategies aiming to restore frataxin expression. These target-engagement biomarkers are valuable in early phases of clinical trials, which mainly aim to demonstrate the biological activity of a treatment before later-phase trials assessing clinical efficacy. Finally, we report on somatic instability in polyglutamine spinocerebellar ataxias as an emerging and highly relevant therapeutic target. CAG repeat mosaicism is gene specific and correlates with disease progression. Integrating measures of repeat instability with neurodegenerative biomarkers could provide a comprehensive monitoring approach in clinical studies. This overview underscores the potential of fluid biomarkers, particularly neurofilament light chain, in accelerating therapeutic development for hereditary ataxias.

primary.title: Post-mortem and high field MRI and MR spectroscopy insights into the neurobiology of autism.
primary.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent challenges in social communication and the presence of restricted, repetitive behaviors. Neuroimaging and post-mortem research have consistently shown that ASD is associated with atypical brain connectivity and microstructural alterations. However, no singular neurobiological marker has been reliably established for diagnosis, and autism diagnoses depend primarily on behavioral evaluations, which may result in delayed or imprecise identification. The biological complexity and heterogeneity of ASD suggest that no single measure is likely to be sufficient, and instead calls for a multidimensional approach that integrates microstructural, neurochemical, and metabolic information. Advanced neuroimaging techniques, particularly ultra-high-field 7 Tesla MRI and phosphorus-31 magnetic resonance spectroscopy (31P MRS), offer promising avenues for detecting subtle neuroanatomical, neurochemical, and metabolic changes in autism. Because studies using 7 T scanners remain sporadic, this review combines a systematic search with a narrative synthesis to assess the current evidence. It brings together post-mortem histological findings with in-vivo ultra-high-field MR evidence across three domains: cortical layer connectivity, excitation-inhibition balance, and bioenergetics. Post-mortem studies establish layer-specific and E/I alterations, while emerging 7 T MRI and MRS findings begin to capture comparable cortical-layer, neurochemical, and bioenergetic differences in living individuals. Because these domains are interdependent, examining them together yields more complete insight than any one in isolation. By showing where these lines of evidence converge, this narrative review identifies directions toward a combination of biologically grounded markers of autism and improved understanding of its neurobiology.

primary.title: Dynamic contributions of astrocytes in Alzheimer's disease.
primary.abstract: In Alzheimer's disease, pathological stimuli reshape astrocyte functions, which in turn act on neurons, making astrocytes critical modulators of disease progression. A comprehensive understanding of how astrocytes dynamically shift from physiology to pathology across multiple functional domains remains to be established. This review synthesizes recent findings across four key domains: proteostasis, gliotransmission/synapse regulation, blood-brain barrier integrity and metabolism, and microglial crosstalk. For each domain, we compare homeostatic and pathological functions, analyze how supportive roles turn detrimental, and discuss effects on neuronal fate. We also examine signaling pathways that govern astrocyte reactivity and the potential of astrocyte-derived biomarkers. By tracing these dynamic transitions, we aim to refine Alzheimer's disease mechanisms and identify state-targeted therapeutic opportunities.

primary.title: Astrocytes in Parkinson's disease: Beyond support, toward therapy.
primary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. While neuronal dysfunction has traditionally been the focal point of PD research, growing evidence highlights the critical roles of astrocytes - the most abundant glial cells in the central nervous system - in PD pathogenesis and therapy. Targeting astrocytes offers a promising therapeutic avenue through astrocyte-to-neuron reprogramming, inducing A2 phenotypic polarization, suppressing oxidative stress, modulating metal ion deposition, enhancing neurotransmitter homeostasis and promoting α-synuclein clearance. These diverse roles enable astrocytes to act as both protectors and potential contributors to disease progression, depending on the cellular environment. Furthermore, innovative strategies such as gene therapy, nanoparticle-based drug delivery, and astrocyte-derived exosome systems hold potential to overcome barriers like the blood-brain barrier and offer targeted, multifactorial interventions. Collectively, these findings advocate for a paradigm shift from a neuron-centric to a glia-inclusive framework in PD research and treatment, positioning astrocytes as central players in the quest for disease-modifying therapies.

primary.title: New insights on microglial lysosomal acidification: A therapeutic target of neurodegenerative diseases.
primary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Microglia, the resident immune cells of the central nervous system (CNS), maintain brain homeostasis and respond to pathological insults. Microglial dysfunction has been implicated in the pathogenesis of several neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis. Impaired lysosomal function, particularly defective lysosomal acidification, leads to the accumulation of undegraded material, thereby promoting neuroinflammation and neuronal damage. PURPOSE: This review examines the mechanisms governing lysosomal acidification in microglia and evaluates its potential as both a therapeutic target and a prognostic biomarker in neurodegenerative diseases. METHODS: The literature on microglial lysosomal acidification, lysosomal pH regulation, autophagy, and neurodegeneration was searched in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. Relevant mechanistic, preclinical, and translational studies were critically appraised and synthesized. RESULTS: Lysosomal acidification is increasingly recognized as a key regulator of microglial function and homeostasis. Defective acidification, driven by dysregulation of the vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) proton pump, TFEB/TFE3 signaling pathways, and lysosomal ion channels such as TRPML1 and TMEM175, impairs autophagic flux and substrate degradation, facilitating the accumulation of neurotoxic aggregates including amyloid-β and α-synuclein. Emerging evidence suggests that the degree of microglial lysosomal acidification may serve as a prognostic biomarker for disease progression and therapeutic response. Restoration or enhancement of lysosomal acidification through pharmacological modulation of lysosomal pH, activation of autophagy, or targeting of key regulatory pathways has been shown to re-establish microglial homeostasis, attenuate neuroinflammation, and confer neuroprotection in preclinical models. CONCLUSION: Restoration of microglial lysosomal acidification represents a promising therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative diseases. A deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms regulating lysosomal acidification in microglia may facilitate the identification of novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets, ultimately contributing to the development of innovative interventions for neurodegenerative disorders.

primary.title: Metabolic reprogramming in diabetic panvascular disease: Molecular mechanism and therapeutic strategies.
primary.abstract: Diabetes mellitus substantially increases the risk of cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, renal, retinal and peripheral vascular complications. These are collectively referred to as diabetic panvascular disease. A traditional approach that treats each complication separately is no longer sufficient. An emerging framework places metabolic reprogramming at its center. This review examines how the diabetic environment, including hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, and dyslipidemia, rewires core metabolic pathways in vascular cells. Major changes include the diversion of glucose through the polyol, hexosamine and AGE-PKC axes, lipotoxicity resulting from excessive fatty acids, disruption of amino acid networks such as BCAA and one-carbon metabolism, mitochondrial dysfunction with increased mtROS production, and epigenetic modifications that drive metabolic memory. These interconnected abnormalities promote oxidative stress and chronic inflammation, which in turn lead to endothelial dysfunction, atherosclerosis, microvascular rarefaction, and end-organ damage in the heart, brain, kidney, retina, and peripheral nerves. We also describe the current therapeutic landscape, ranging from established agents such as metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, RAAS blockers, and anti-VEGF therapies to emerging mechanism-based strategies including aldose reductase inhibitors, glucokinase activators, PKC, RAGE, NOX, and NLRP3 inhibitors, miRNA modulators, and exosome therapy. Finally, we highlight unmet needs and future directions. These may include multi-omics guided precision phenotyping, cross-organ causal inference, single-cell metabolic flux technologies, and adaptive clinical trial designs. By shifting from a glucose-centric to a metabolic reprogramming-centric paradigm, this review aims to provide a roadmap for developing more targeted therapies for diabetic panvascular disease.

primary.title: C-fiber low-threshold mechanoreceptors versus C-fiber nociceptors: distinct properties and signatures.
primary.abstract: Mammalian skin is innervated by distinct classes of low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs) and nociceptors, which are broadly categorized according to axonal conduction velocity into Aβ-, Aδ-and C-fiber populations. C-LTMRs encode innocuous mechanical stimuli and, in humans (where they are termed C-tactile [CT] afferents), contribute to affective/social touch, whereas nociceptors detect potentially tissue-damaging stimuli. For decades, C-LTMRs were thought to be confined to hairy skin. However, approximately a decade ago, we provided the first electrophysiological evidence for a rare population of C-LTMRs in rat glabrous skin. Subsequent human studies identified sparse CT afferents in the palm, indicating that C-LTMRs are present in glabrous skin in both rodents and humans, albeit far less frequently than in hairy skin. This review examines evidence supporting the presence and conservation of C-LTMRs across species in both hairy and glabrous skin, and that they are molecularly, anatomically, transcriptionally, and functionally distinct from C-fiber nociceptors, differing in their peripheral endings, central projections, receptive properties, and electrophysiological signatures. We also critically examine the proposed state-dependent role of C-LTMRs in injury-induced mechanical hypersensitivity, highlighting conflicting evidence from VGLUT3-based studies and emphasizing that their causal contribution to pathological pain remains unresolved. In contrast, under homeostatic conditions, C-LTMRs may instead engage inhibitory spinal microcircuits and release anti-nociceptive mediators, such as TAFA4, that help limit hypersensitivity. We summarize the ion channels and neurochemical markers that distinguish C-LTMRs from C-nociceptors and discuss how failure to recognize these distinct afferent populations may lead to misinterpretation of somatosensory and pain-related findings.

primary.title: Cytoskeletal alterations underlying dendritic and synaptic plasticity in epilepsy.
primary.abstract: Aberrant dendritic changes in epilepsy, morphologically measured by the complexity and length of dendrite, as well as the density of dendritic spines, are dynamic and various considering disease course, developmental stages, and various neuronal type across different brain regions. Correspondingly, imbalanced excitatory and inhibitory synapses in epilepsy, quantitatively measured by the expression level and location of synaptic proteins, still vary considering etiology, disease course, and brain regions. And, various mechanisms involved in synaptic pruning add to the complexity of synaptic alterations in epilepsy. Still, sharing mechanisms underlying aberrant dendritic and synaptic plasticity in epilepsy exist, and cytoskeletal alterations can serve as a tool to decipher alterations of dendritic morphology and synaptic plasticity in epilepsy. Evidences supporting aberrant microtubule dynamics and post-translational modifications of tubulin in epilepsy emerge, combined with their involvement in dendritic morphology and synaptic plasticity. In conclusion, this review respectively summarizes the characteristics of dendritic pathology, synaptic alterations, microtubule dynamics, and tubulin's post-translational modifications in epilepsy, and discusses their interplay and correlation in epilepsy, providing insight into how cytoskeletal organization contributes to macroscopic changes in epilepsy.

primary.title: Mesenchymal stem cell-derived secretome in traumatic brain injury: Stage-specific paracrine mechanisms and translational challenges.
primary.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a stage-dependent disorder that evolves from acute neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, oxidative stress, excitotoxicity, and apoptosis to subacute neurovascular remodeling and chronic impairment of neuroregeneration and circuit repair. Current clinical management improves survival by stabilizing physiological status and limiting secondary injury, but it rarely rebuilds damaged neural networks or restores long-term neurological function. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have therefore attracted attention as regenerative candidates, with increasing evidence indicating that their benefits are mediated mainly by paracrine mechanisms rather than direct neuronal replacement. This review presents the MSC-derived secretome as a multilayered therapeutic system composed of soluble mediators and extracellular vesicles (EVs), the latter serving as carriers of proteins, lipids, messenger RNAs (mRNAs), microRNAs (miRNAs), and other regulatory cargoes. Instead of listing isolated cytokines, growth factors, or chemokines, we organize MSC paracrine mechanisms by TBI stage: acute neuroprotection, subacute vascular and immune remodeling, and chronic neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, and network repair. We also clarify the relationship between EVs and their cargoes and compare the evidence levels for exosomes, microvesicles, and apoptotic bodies. Finally, we discuss translational barriers, including secretome heterogeneity, therapeutic-window optimization, delivery efficiency, bioengineering approaches, and clinical translation.

secondary.title: Tumor innervation in non-central nervous system tumors: origins, mechanisms, and phenotypic plasticity.
secondary.abstract: The peripheral nervous system has emerged as an important regulator of solid tumor biology. We synthesize recent advances in cancer neuroscience, focusing on three interconnected themes: the cellular origins of tumor-associated nerves, the molecular mechanisms that govern neural recruitment and remodeling, and the resulting phenotypic plasticity within the tumor microenvironment. Tumor innervation arises through axon extension from pre-existing nerves, recruitment of neural precursors, and neuron-like transdifferentiation of non-neuronal cells. These processes are driven by neurotrophic factors, axon guidance cues, extracellular vesicles, and stress-associated pathways. The functional consequences of innervation are context-dependent, with sympathetic, parasympathetic, and sensory inputs exerting distinct effects across tumor types and stages. We conclude by outlining key challenges and future directions for therapeutic translation.

secondary.title: Modeling Moyamoya disease using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells and organoids.
secondary.abstract: The underlying mechanisms of Moyamoya disease (MMD), a rare, progressive cerebrovascular disorder marked by distal internal carotid artery stenosis or occlusion and the formation of fragile collaterals, remain poorly understood, in part because conventional models fail to capture the genetic, vascular, and neurovascular complexity of human MMD. Driven by recent advances in disease modeling, MMD research has moved beyond early endothelial progenitor cell studies toward patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based platforms. Here, we summarize the generation and validation of MMD-specific iPSCs and their differentiation into endothelial cells (ECs), vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and related vascular lineages, and we discuss how two-dimensional (2D) iPSC-based models have provided insights into impaired angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, abnormal VSMC behavior, and disrupted vascular cell interactions. We then highlight the emerging use of three-dimensional vascular and neurovascular organoids, which reproduce cellular heterogeneity, vessel-like organization, and neurovascular unit interactions more closely than conventional 2D cultures. These models may provide a more integrated platform for investigating the complex vascular pathophysiology of MMD. Finally, we discuss future directions for MMD modeling, including the integration of multi-omics profiling and CRISPR-mediated genome editing with patient-derived iPSC and organoid platforms. These approaches may help clarify genotype-phenotype relationships, RNF213-dependent and RNF213-independent mechanisms, and disease-relevant molecular pathways. With further standardization and validation, iPSC- and organoid-based models could support mechanistic studies, therapeutic screening, and personalized disease modeling. Our review underscores the emerging role of patient-derived stem cell and organoid technologies in advancing MMD research and in informing future translational efforts.

secondary.title: Lysosomal dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease.
secondary.abstract: Examination of genetic risk factors associated with neurodegenerative diseases has provided important mechanistic insights into the pathophysiology of these disorders, and it has implicated defects in lysosomal function as a key component of the neurodegenerative process. The lysosome has a primary role in mediating degradation of both intracellular contents and endocytosed material from the extracellular space. Aggregation of misfolded proteins is a pathological mechanism that is observed across neurodegenerative disorders, and aberrant lysosomal degradation of such proteins plays a pivotal part in driving neuronal dysfunction and cell loss. In addition to the crucial role of the endolysosomal system in degradation of intracellular constituents, lysosomes also serve as important nodes for intracellular signalling, participating in nutrient sensing, lipid metabolism, membrane repair and neuroinflammation. In this Review, we provide an overview of mechanisms of lysosomal dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease, with a particular focus on Parkinson disease, Alzheimer disease, frontotemporal dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

secondary.title: Achieving High Spatial Resolution Transmission Electron Microscopy Studies in Closed Liquid Cells.
secondary.abstract: Liquid cell transmission electron microscopy (LCTEM) is a rising technique for probing dynamic processes and structural transformations in liquid environments at the nanoscale. However, its broader application is largely constrained by limited spatial resolution, which arises from electron scattering by the encapsulating membranes and the liquid layer. Recent advances in instrument design, micro-electro-mechanical system (MEMS)-based cells, and ultrathin window materials have substantially improved imaging quality, yet achieving atomic-scale resolution in liquids remains a formidable challenge. This review provides a comprehensive overview of such strategies developed to enhance the spatial resolution of LCTEM, emphasizing the roles of liquid layer thickness, MEMS design, and cell configuration. We highlight representative approaches, such as reducing liquid and membrane thicknesses, optimizing MEMS architectures, and employing grid-based liquid cells, and discuss their underlying mechanisms and recent progress. Finally, we outline current challenges and future opportunities for achieving high-resolution, multifunctional LCTEM systems capable of capturing dynamic processes in realistic liquid environments.

secondary.title: Secondary electron imaging in transmission electron microscopy: technique and application in nanocatalysis.
secondary.abstract: The determination of the smallest structures and surface morphologies of nanoparticles using Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) is widely regarded as one of the most essential techniques for modern researchers. Despite its proven scientific effectiveness, TEM has certain limitations, the main one of which is that the analysis of nanoparticles or their agglomerates - in fact three-dimensional structures - results in two-dimensional images, which may not fully reflect their complex geometries. A promising solution to this problem lies in the integrated on modern TEM devices secondary electron (SE) detectors. These detectors, optimized for capturing low-energy secondary electrons, function similarly to those in Scanning Electron Microscopy. Complementing high-resolution TEM or STEM images, the SE detector provides three-dimensional images with a resolution close to or equal to atomic, while allowing avoidance of the labor-intensive and time-consuming processes associated with TEM-based 3D tomography, for example. With current advancements in detector technology, secondary electron imaging holds significant potential as a primary tool for investigating the morphology of a wide spectrum of nanomaterials, including nanoparticles and powders, paving the way for broader applications in nanoscience and materials research. In this review, we will briefly cover the features of the method and its main physical principles, and recent advances in its application in nanocatalysis with platinum group metals-based catalysts, where the application of this method could be revolutionary. The distribution of metal nanoparticles on the carbon or other support is a critical factor directly affecting the performance of these materials. And, as practice shows, traditional TEM often fails to provide comprehensive information on their morphology.

secondary.title: Geographic patterns of asthma morbidity: a systematic review of Sand and dust storm (SDS) impacts in Asia.
secondary.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Sand and Dust Storms (SDS) are prevalent in Asia, releasing fine particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5) that pose significant risks to respiratory health, particularly for asthmatic populations. This systematic review evaluates the impact of SDS on asthma incidence, hospital admissions, and exacerbations across Asia, providing a basis for public health interventions. DATA SOURCES: We performed a systematic search in PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published up to May 2023 using terms related to sand and dust storms, SDS, asthma, and respiratory health. STUDY SELECTION: Thirty-three studies met the inclusion criteria, predominantly from Japan, Korea, and the Middle East. Cohort (n = 13; 39.4%) and panel designs (n = 12; 36.4%) were the frequent methodologies. RESULTS: Findings consistently revealed a significant association between SDS and increased asthma exacerbations, hospital admissions, and emergency visits, peaking within 1-5 days post-exposure. Overall, the vast majority of the evaluated studies documented a positive association between SDS and asthma-related healthcare utilization, although the magnitude and statistical significance varied according to study designs and outcome definitions. The impact was disproportionately high among children and the elderly. Notably, studies from East Asia demonstrated more pronounced health impacts, including higher odds ratios and longer hospital stays, compared to the Middle East. CONCLUSION: SDS are a significant burden on respiratory health in Asia. Our findings underscore the need for targeted, region-specific public health strategies and improved air quality monitoring. However, results are subject to limitations, including significant study heterogeneity and potential language bias due to the exclusion of non-English publications.

secondary.title: Dysfunction of lipid metabolism and lysosomal capacity: at the core of microglial aging?
secondary.abstract: As primary immune cells of the central nervous system (CNS), microglia maintain immune surveillance, inflammation regulation, cell interactions and debris clearance. These dynamic and adaptive effector functions are reciprocally sustained by microglial metabolism. Lipids are emerging as a key programmer of microglial metabolic and functional flexibility in conditions of homeostasis, cellular stress, and pathology. The delicate equilibrium in microglial lipid homeostasis is dependent on the integrated activity of all cellular components, including the lysosome-lipophagy pathway. Continuous adaptations in microglial metabolism contribute to a cumulative imbalance between lysosomal network capacity and the efficacy of lipid turnover in aged microglia. The disequilibrium contributes to microglial fatigue and detrimental homeostatic activity associated with aging. Lipid droplet-accumulating microglia (LDAM) emerged as an age-associated example of these lysosome-lipid flux alterations. While characterized by dysregulated phagocytosis and pro-inflammatory intercellular signaling, the role of LDAM in the contexts of neuroplasticity, aging-related cognitive decline and frailty remains undetermined. This review discusses the immunometabolic profile of aging LDAM and their interactions with neurons and synapses, highlighting the impact of intercellular lipid signaling route.

secondary.title: Modeling human neurodegeneration with iPSCs: opportunities, limitations, and the challenge of aging.
secondary.abstract: Most neurodegenerative diseases reflect patient-specific combinations of polygenic risk variants interacting with aging and environmental factors, rather than a single causative mutation. Phase III clinical trial failure rates for neurodegenerative indications exceed 95%, reflecting in part the limitations of existing preclinical systems to fully model the human genetic context of disease. Patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have the potential to address this shortcoming by faithfully recapitulating human cell biology and preserving each patient's complete genetic architecture. This Review examines iPSC-based models of neurodegeneration across three themes. First, we discuss mechanisms revealed by these models, from convergent pathways uncovered by familial mutations to early evidence that sporadic disease biology is accessible at sufficient cohort scale. Second, we evaluate culture systems from 2-dimensional monocultures to organoids, examining how increasing complexity expands addressable biological questions while introducing trade-offs. Third, we address the aging problem: reprogramming erases epigenetic signatures of donor aging, removing the cellular context in which late-onset sporadic neurodegeneration emerges. We discuss strategies approximating aging in iPSC-derived neurons and highlight direct conversion strategies that preserve native epigenetic age, enabling access to age-dependent phenotypes. We propose a framework matching model systems to biological questions, improving mechanistic understanding and therapeutic development.

secondary.title: The translational asymmetry of corpus callosotomy: Two literatures that answered different questions.
secondary.abstract: Corpus callosotomy is an established palliative operation for drug-resistant epilepsy dominated by drop attacks, and it is performed in three extents: anterior, usually of the anterior two-thirds; total, in one or two stages; and selective posterior, which preserves the genu and rostral body. Meta-analysis finds no difference between them in overall seizure reduction, a difference in drop attack control favoring the posterior approach, and a graded difference in disconnection syndrome, but there has never been a prospective head-to-head comparison, and the optimal extent of section remains undefined. A search of PubMed, Embase, and the Web of Science Core Collection identified 62 experimental studies in which the corpus callosum or another forebrain commissure was sectioned with an epilepsy-related outcome, spanning 1948-2026 across six species and every major seizure model. This literature is neither absent nor recent. What it has almost never done is vary the extent of section: the few studies that varied it took the laterality of kindling transfer or of interictal synchrony as the endpoint, never seizure control and never cognitive cost. No study compares the three extents against a common outcome; none models the selective posterior operation as it is defined clinically; none randomizes between extents; and none combines graded disconnection with time-locked bilateral electrophysiology, diffusion-based verification of the fibers divided, and a behavioral read-out in the same animals. The effect of section is also bidirectional: focal seizures may intensify through loss of transcallosal inhibition, and in the pentylenetetrazol model callosal section paradoxically facilitates convulsions, which limits chemoconvulsant preparations. The asymmetry between the clinical and experimental literatures is therefore one of method rather than of volume or attention: the two answered different questions, and the question the clinical field now asks requires a manipulation the experimental literature has never performed. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Surgeons can treat severe epilepsies by cutting the bundle of fibers that joins the two halves of the brain, but they do not agree on how much of it to cut. We searched three databases and found 62 animal studies of this operation going back to 1948. Almost none of them compared different amounts of cutting, and none looked at the newest version of the operation. Answering the surgeons' question will require a new kind of animal experiment rather than more reading of the old ones.

secondary.title: Human erythroid models of sickle cell disease.
secondary.abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a group of severe inherited red blood cell disorders causing a major global healthcare burden. Despite recent advances in gene therapy and stem cell transplantation, treatment options remain very limited, highlighting the urgent need for the development of new therapeutic approaches. Human erythroid model systems of SCD represent emerging tools for the discovery of disease-modifying strategies through drug screening and mechanistic studies. This review describes the range of models available, including patient-derived red blood cells, hematopoietic stem cells, induced pluripotent stem cells, and immortalized cell lines, and summarizes their relative advantages and disadvantages, as well as potential integration with more complex integrated co-culture and organoid models. Overall, these cellular systems represent an expanding toolkit available to SCD researchers with the potential to reduce reliance on the use of animal models.

secondary.title: From iPSC disease modeling to epigenome editing: Toward therapeutic reversal of genomic imprinting disorders.
secondary.abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and organoids are increasingly important components of new approach methodologies because they provide experimentally accessible human systems that preserve patient-specific genetic backgrounds and can be differentiated into disease-relevant cell types. Genomic imprinting disorders are particularly attractive targets for this approach because their pathogenesis depends not only on DNA sequence but also on parent-of-origin-specific epigenetic regulation. Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) and Angelman syndrome (AS), which arise from distinct disruptions within the same imprinted domain on chromosome 15q11.2-q13, illustrate both the opportunities and the complexity of therapeutic epigenetic manipulation. Recent studies using PWS patient-derived iPSCs have shown that disease-associated imprinting states are largely retained after reprogramming and can be experimentally reversed by locus-specific epigenome editing. Targeted demethylation of the PWS imprinting control region restored multiple paternally expressed genes, and the corrected state persisted after differentiation into hypothalamic organoids, partially normalizing disease-associated transcriptomic and functional phenotypes. Here, we discuss how iPSC-based disease modeling is evolving from a platform for mechanism discovery toward a test bed for therapeutic epigenome engineering and outline the major challenges that must be addressed before epigenome editing can be translated to patients with imprinting disorders.

secondary.title: Lysosomes as chemical and metabolic organizers of central nervous system injury and repair.
secondary.abstract: Lysosomes are degradative, metabolic and signaling organelles in central nervous system (CNS) cells and play essential roles in neural homeostasis, injury responses and disease progression. Changes in lysosomal function are required for neurons, microglia, astrocytes and oligodendrocyte-lineage cells to adapt to proteotoxic stress, lipid overload, mitochondrial damage and inflammatory stimulation. Therefore, lysosomal activity in the CNS is regulated by diverse chemical and cellular cues, including luminal acidification, hydrolase maturation, ion transport, membrane integrity, lipid handling and transcriptional lysosome biogenesis. Here, we summarize current knowledge of lysosomal organization and function in neural cells, including lysosomal membrane signaling, vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase)-dependent acidification, ion and redox regulation, lysosomal membrane quality control, and metabolic recycling of proteins, lipids, glycans and damaged organelles. We then survey pathological lysosomal remodeling in spinal cord injury, traumatic brain injury, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and related neurological disorders. Across these conditions, lysosomal remodeling may initially support cargo clearance and stress adaptation, but becomes maladaptive when degradative capacity, membrane repair or lipid-processing ability fails to meet cellular demand. Finally, we discuss lysosome-oriented therapeutic strategies for neural repair, including restoration of lysosomal acidification and hydrolase activity, transcription factor EB/transcription factor E3 (TFEB/TFE3)-mediated lysosomal biogenesis, regulation of lysosomal ion channels, enhancement of myelin lipid turnover, and lysosome-responsive nanomedicine. This Review highlights lysosomes as active organizers of CNS injury and repair rather than passive endpoints of degradation.

secondary.title: Engineered Vascularization: Neurovascular Niche Remodeling Enables Biomimetic Brain Organoids for Central Nervous System Research.
secondary.abstract: Preclinical central nervous system (CNS) disease models face a persistent translational gap arising from interspecies differences and limited representation of the human neurovascular microenvironment. Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived brain organoids provide a human-relevant platform for modeling brain development and disease, but limited vascularization restricts tissue growth, maturation, and neurovascular function. Engineering approaches, including genetic engineering, biomaterials, 3D bioprinting, and organ-on-a-chip technologies, enable greater control over vascular specification, spatial organization, extracellular matrix properties, and perfusion, facilitating more controlled remodeling of the neurovascular niche. This Review summarizes recent advances in engineered vascularization of brain organoids, focusing on engineering strategies, biological outcomes, and applications in neurodevelopmental research, CNS disease modeling, and preclinical drug screening. Particular emphasis is placed on evaluating vascularization using complementary evidence rather than individual vascular markers. Based on quantitative data from 13 published studies, we propose the Multidimensional Quality Assessment Framework for Vascularized Brain Organoids (MQAF-VBO) and highlight relationships between engineering parameters and biological outcomes. Emerging opportunities in nanoengineered biomaterials, programmable platforms, spatial profiling, integrated biosensing, and adaptive bioelectronic systems are also discussed. Collectively, these advances may facilitate the development of more reproducible and physiologically relevant vascularized brain organoids for CNS disease modeling and preclinical drug evaluation.

secondary.title: Bidirectional Regulatory Mechanisms of T cell-microglia Interactions in Cerebral Ischemic Disease: Molecular Crosstalk, Experimental Techniques and Therapeutic Implications.
secondary.abstract: Cerebral ischemic diseases, such as ischemic stroke (IS) and vascular dementia (VaD), are major causes of neurological disability and mortality. Neuroinflammation acts as a pivotal driver of secondary brain injury, mediated by intricate bidirectional interactions between peripheral T cells and central nervous system (CNS)-resident microglia. This review delineates the molecular mechanisms underlying T cell-microglia crosstalk in cerebral ischemia, emphasizing their dual roles in exacerbating neurotoxicity and promoting repair. Direct interactions involve antigen presentation via MHC-TCR engagement and co-stimulatory checkpoints (e.g., CD80/CD86-CD28, PD-L1-PD-1), which regulate T cell activation and microglial polarization. Direct signaling through cytokines (IFN-γ, IL-4, IL-17, IL-10) further modulates microglial phenotypes: Th1/Th17 cells drive pro-inflammatory M1 polarization via STAT1/NF-κB pathways, while Tregs/Th2 cells induce anti-inflammatory M2 states through STAT6/SMAD signaling. Spatial transcriptomics and single-cell omics reveal spatiotemporal dynamics of these interactions, identifying STAT1/STAT6 imbalance as a critical determinant of neuroinflammatory outcomes. Advanced methodologies, including two-photon intravital microscopy and microfluidic blood-brain barrier (BBB) models, enable real-time visualization of immune cell trafficking and synaptic communication. Therapeutically, targeting immune checkpoints (CTLA-4, PD-1) or cytokine pathways (e.g., IL-4 mimetics) shows promise in recalibrating neuroimmune responses. However, challenges such as blood-brain barrier impermeability to biologics and interspecies immune heterogeneity necessitate innovative delivery strategies. This review integrates molecular, cellular, and technological insights to propose a framework for precision immunomodulation. By elucidating context-dependent signaling nodes and leveraging emerging tools, the study underscores the potential of harnessing T cell-microglia crosstalk to mitigate neuroinflammation and enhance neural repair, offering transformative avenues for stroke and dementia therapy.

secondary.title: From Intestinal Origins to Mammary Targets: Exploring the Potential Role of the Brain-Gut-Microbiota Axis in Pre-Metastatic Conditioning of Breast Tissue in Colorectal Cancer.
secondary.abstract: Historically viewed as a localized gastrointestinal malignancy, colorectal cancer (CRC) is increasingly recognized as a systemic pathology that actively programs distant microenvironments. This review delineates a novel mechanistic framework wherein CRC-driven dysregulation of the brain-gut-microbiota axis (BGMA) acts as a systemic architect of the breast pre-metastatic niche (PMN). We synthesize how localized intestinal oncogenic stress propagates through three convergent conduits: (1) Immune Reprogramming, where gut-derived inflammatory mediators and extracellular vesicles (EVs) recruit myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) to the mammary stroma; (2) Neuro-ecological Conditioning, involving chronic hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis activation and sympathetic hyperactivation that drives catecholamine-mediated remodeling of breast tissue; and (3) Humoral-Metabolic Convergence, specifically via the "estrobolome" and secondary bile acids that synchronize systemic hormonal levels with local tissue receptivity. By reframing CRC progression as a systemic pathology that potentially preconditions distant, hormone-sensitive environments, we propose the BGMA as a conceptual framework for prospective "systemic interception", outlining roadmaps to neutralize metastatic cascades at their incipient, reversible stages.

secondary.title: The Role of Astrocytes in the Inflammatory Response in Neurodiseases.
secondary.abstract: Astrocytes have emerged as central regulators of neuroinflammation, extending far beyond their traditional roles as structural and metabolic support cells. In neurological disorders, astrocytes undergo reactive remodeling that encompasses morphological, transcriptional, metabolic, and functional changes. Rather than fitting into a fixed A1/A2 dichotomy, reactive astrocytes exist along a disease-, region-, and stage-dependent continuum shaped by local pathology and intercellular crosstalk. This review summarizes how astrocytes contribute to neuroinflammatory processes in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, central nervous system injury, infection, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorder. We highlight convergent mechanisms, including cytokine and chemokine release, complement activation, glutamate and ion homeostasis disruption, oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming, and blood-brain barrier regulation, while emphasizing disease-specific astrocytic programs. We further discuss astrocyte interactions with microglia, neurons, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, as well as key regulatory pathways, epigenetic remodeling, and lipid-dependent metabolic signaling. Finally, we evaluate current and emerging astrocyte-targeted therapeutic strategies, including metabolic modulation, receptor targeting, gene editing, nanodelivery, and gut-brain axis interventions. Defining functionally validated astrocyte states and developing biomarker-guided, stage-adaptive therapies may enable more precise intervention in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases.

secondary.title: Animal models for investigating post-stroke cognitive impairment: A neurovascular trafficking perspective.
secondary.abstract: Post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) is a major cause of long-term disability after ischemic stroke, yet its mechanisms remain incompletely explained by infarct volume, lesion location, or conventional vascular risk factors alone. Animal models are indispensable for clarifying how ischemic injury evolves into delayed cognitive dysfunction and for determining which mechanisms are experimentally tractable, reproducible, and translationally relevant. This review examines PSCI from a neurovascular trafficking perspective, focusing on how laboratory animal models can be used to investigate secretory pathway stress, endolysosomal dysfunction, autophagy-lysosomal flux, extracellular vesicle signaling, blood-brain barrier disruption, glial reactivity, myelin debris clearance, white matter injury, and cognition-relevant behavioral phenotypes. Rodent models of transient or permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion, photothrombotic stroke, embolic stroke, chronic cerebral hypoperfusion, bilateral carotid artery stenosis, and subcortical white-matter injury each reproduce selected components of the human PSCI spectrum. No single model fully captures the temporal, vascular, cellular, and cognitive complexity of human PSCI; therefore, model selection should be driven by the mechanistic question, disease phase, vascular pathology, cellular compartment, cognitive domain, and welfare burden under investigation. The central argument is not that neurovascular trafficking failure is already a proven causal pathway, but that well-designed animal studies can test, refine, or falsify this hypothesis. Future studies should integrate model validity, translational rigor, and welfare refinement through longitudinal cognitive testing, multimodal imaging, cell-specific molecular profiling, extracellular vesicle phenotyping, intervention-based validation, randomization, blinding, sample-size justification, humane endpoints, perioperative care, and transparent reporting.

secondary.title: Central neuroendocrine governance as a unifying framework for host-tumor interaction: From afferent sensing to therapeutic modulation.
secondary.abstract: Cancer is not biologically confined to the tumor bed. Cachexia, fatigue, metabolic dysfunction, circadian disruption, and immune dysfunction reflect disturbances that local models alone cannot fully explain. The brain is well positioned to participate in these processes because it continuously samples circulating signals and coordinates endocrine and autonomic responses. Yet the afferent side of this communication has received less attention than its downstream consequences. Here, we synthesize evidence showing that cytokines, hormones, metabolites, and cargo carried by extracellular vesicles can engage central sensory interfaces and integrative regions, particularly circumventricular organs and hypothalamic and brainstem circuits. We use the term Endocriception to describe afferent humoral sensing and early central decoding of circulating biochemical signals, and focus here on how tumor- and host-associated changes engage this process in cancer. Central neuroendocrine governance refers to the subsequent integration of this information and the generation of autonomic and endocrine outputs. Persistent inflammation, stress, circadian disruption, and impaired feedback may gradually reconfigure this regulatory system. The resulting changes can affect systemic immunity, metabolism, behavior, and host tolerance of cancer. Evidence is strongest for a limited number of pathways, whereas many proposed links remain incomplete or dependent on tumor type and experimental context. We therefore present central neuroendocrine governance as a working framework for organizing current evidence and guiding mechanistic studies, biomarker development, and interventions aimed at restoring host physiology.

secondary.title: Why does siRNA delivery still fail in neurodegenerative diseases? Biological barriers, nanocarrier engineering, and future translational directions.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases remain largely untreatable at the disease-modifying level, with currently approved therapies providing primarily symptomatic benefits. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) has emerged as a promising therapeutic modality because of its ability to selectively silence disease-associated genes. However, a major obstacle to clinical translation is not the gene-silencing mechanism itself, but the efficient delivery of therapeutic siRNAs to target cells within the central nervous system.This review examines the barriers that limit siRNA-based therapies for neurodegenerative diseases. We adopt a barrier-oriented framework that follows the sequential challenges encountered during siRNA delivery, including extracellular instability, unfavorable pharmacokinetics, immune recognition, limited transport across the blood-brain barrier, inefficient cellular internalization, and endosomal entrapment. Rather than cataloguing available delivery systems, we evaluate how nanocarrier engineering strategies have been developed to address these barriers and assess their impact on delivery. Evidence from Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease is synthesized to distinguish shared limitations from disease-specific challenges and to evaluate the translational performance of lipid-based nanoparticles, polymeric nanocarriers, engineered exosomes, and hybrid platforms.Available evidence indicates that delivery platforms can improve specific aspects of siRNA transport but have not consistently overcome the sequential biological barriers required for therapy. Although nanocarrier engineering has enhanced siRNA stability, brain targeting, intracellular trafficking, and gene-silencing efficiency in preclinical models, manufacturing scalability, biological heterogeneity, long-term safety, reproducibility, and regulatory feasibility remain important barriers to clinical translation. Future progress will likely depend on delivery systems that integrate effective brain transport, endosomal escape, controlled intracellular release, and scalable manufacturing within clinical platforms.

secondary.title: Fluorogenic RNA aptamers in cancer: emerging platforms for molecular imaging, biosensing, and precision oncology.
secondary.abstract: Fluorogenic RNA aptamers have emerged as powerful molecular tools for cancer imaging, biosensing, and biomarker detection due to their high specificity, low background fluorescence, and genetic encodability. These short RNA molecules activate fluorescence upon binding specific fluorogens, enabling real-time visualization of intracellular targets and dynamic molecular processes in living systems. Recent advances in RNA structural engineering, fluorophore optimization, and biosensor integration have significantly expanded the translational applications of fluorogenic aptamers in oncology. This mini-review summarizes the structural principles, fluorescence activation mechanisms, and cancer-related applications of fluorogenic RNA aptamers and related nucleic acid biosensors. Foundational studies describing the architecture of fluorogenic aptamer families, including Spinach, Broccoli, Mango, Pepper, Squash, and Beetroot, are discussed with emphasis on G-quadruplex-mediated fluorogen stabilization and fluorescence enhancement. Furthermore, recent developments in CRISPR/Cas-assisted fluorogenic biosensors, dual-color RNA imaging systems, fluorogenic DNAzymes, and amplification-driven aptamer platforms are highlighted. Direct applications across multiple malignancies, including brain, breast, colorectal, liver, lung, prostate, and skin cancers, demonstrate the growing utility of these technologies for tumor-associated RNA detection, epigenetic biomarker analysis, molecular imaging, and therapeutic monitoring. In addition, advances in fluorescence brightness, structural stability, and multiplex imaging strategies have improved the sensitivity and adaptability of fluorogenic RNA systems for complex biological environments. Despite current limitations related to RNA stability, intracellular delivery, and tissue penetration, fluorogenic RNA aptamers represent highly promising tools for next-generation precision oncology. Continued integration with nanotechnology, live-cell imaging, artificial intelligence, and molecular diagnostics is expected to enhance further their clinical and translational potential in cancer research and personalized medicine.

secondary.title: The small giant actor in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases: Microtubules.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a clinically and pathologically diverse group of disorders characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, synaptic impairment, and neuronal loss. Although research has traditionally focused on disease-associated protein misfolding and aggregation, increasing evidence implicates abnormalities of cytoskeletal organization and intracellular transport in several neurodegenerative conditions. Microtubules contribute to neuronal polarity, axonal and dendritic transport, organelle distribution, and synaptic maintenance. These functions are regulated in part by tubulin isotypes, post-translational modifications collectively described as the tubulin code, microtubule-associated proteins, and molecular motors. This narrative review examines evidence linking alterations in these processes with Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and prion disease. We summarize proposed interactions among microtubule instability, impaired axonal transport, mitochondrial dysfunction, and disease-associated proteins, including tau, α-synuclein, mutant huntingtin, TDP-43, and prion protein. Evidence connecting tau pathology with microtubule dysfunction is comparatively well established in Alzheimer's disease and MAPT-related tauopathies, whereas findings in other disorders are more heterogeneous and are frequently derived from cellular or animal models. We also discuss emerging experimental approaches, candidate biomarkers, and investigational microtubule-directed treatments. However, no tubulin-specific biomarker or microtubule-targeted disease-modifying treatment discussed in this review has yet been clinically validated. Overall, microtubule dysfunction may represent one component of broader, disease-specific pathological networks rather than a universal primary cause of neurodegeneration. Further longitudinal and clinical studies are needed to determine whether microtubule-related alterations act as causes, consequences, or modifiers of disease progression.

secondary.title: Autophagy-Modulating Nanomedicine for Glioma: Delivery Barriers, Lysosomal Interactions, and a Flux-Resolved Translational Decision Framework.
secondary.abstract: Glioma nanomedicine is constrained by linked delivery and pharmacodynamic barriers: nanoscale systems must traverse heterogeneous blood-brain barrier (BBB) and blood-brain tumor barrier (BBTB) interfaces and achieve interpretable intracellular effects in tumor cells. Autophagy is a therapeutically relevant but context-dependent axis. However, similar changes in static autophagy markers, vesicular staining, or ultrastructure can reflect productive autophagy induction (ie, increased autophagic flux with successful lysosomal cargo degradation), blocked autophagosome-lysosome fusion, lysosomal dysfunction, or secondary cytotoxic stress. This ambiguity is amplified for nanomedicines because their physicochemical properties can independently shape autophagy-related readouts. Here, we frame autophagy-modulating nanomedicine for glioma as both a delivery challenge and a problem of translational interpretation, covering bioactive nanomaterials, nanocarriers, and multimodal platforms. We organize the field around an integrated framework linking BBB/BBTB access, intracellular trafficking, interpretation of autophagic flux, and translational readiness. We use structured evidence grading to distinguish flux-resolved, functionally validated mechanisms from marker-based or indirect inferences. This framework distinguishes mechanistically supported findings from provisional interpretations and defines the evidence required for translational progression.

secondary.title: From patient cells to patient therapy: Twenty years of iPSC-based translation in neurodegenerative disease.
secondary.abstract: Twenty years after the discovery of induced pluripotent stem cells, the field has progressed from patient-specific disease modeling toward cell-based therapies for neurodegenerative disorders. Parkinson's disease has emerged as the leading model for neuronal replacement, whereas Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis require distinct combinations of circuit reconstruction, cellular support, immune modulation, and engineered therapeutic delivery. We discuss key determinants of clinical translation, including cell source, product identity, graft composition, graft-host interactions, manufacturing reproducibility, genomic integrity, and clinical evaluation. We propose that the interval between cell transplantation and long-term engraftment constitutes a biological "black box" in which graft fate and therapeutic outcome are determined. As regenerative medicine enters its third decade, future progress will depend not only on generating therapeutic cells but also on elucidating and engineering the biological processes that determine their fate after transplantation, marking a conceptual transition from stem cell biology toward transplantation biology.

secondary.title: Human iPSC models of myocardial infarction: From injury to repair and therapeutic discovery.
secondary.abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) remains a leading cause of death worldwide, and therapies that limit injury, promote repair, and restore cardiac function remain limited. Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) provide a renewable source of patient-specific cardiac cells and have enabled the development of increasingly complex in vitro models that incorporate cardiomyocytes together with supporting stromal and vascular cell types. These models are now being used to study multiple stages of MI pathophysiology and are increasingly being applied in therapeutic discovery and regenerative strategies. In this review, we summarize hiPSC-based cardiac models spanning 2D cultures to advanced 3D tissues, organoids, and heart-on-chip systems, evaluating how well they capture key features of human MI. We further discuss hiPSC applications in therapeutic discovery, drug screening, precision medicine, and regenerative repair. Finally, we highlight priorities for the field, including improved physiological complexity, stronger translational robustness, bioengineering strategies, and integration with multi-omics.

secondary.title: iPSC-derived retinal organoids: Biological insights and progress toward photoreceptor replacement therapy.
secondary.abstract: Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived retinal organoids (ROs) have emerged as a platform for photoreceptor replacement therapy, supported by two complementary approaches: cone precursor cell transplantation and RO transplantation. Both have demonstrated proof of concept for functional synaptic integration with the host retinal network, with the first clinical application of iPSC-derived RO transplantation conducted in 2020. Key mechanistic insights include the role of the host environment in cone integration, genome editing-based enhancement of host-graft synaptogenesis recapitulating developmental synaptic assembly, and synaptic rewiring capacity in the adult primate retina. Beyond biology, successful clinical translation requires establishing meaningful endpoints that reflect stepwise therapeutic improvement, scalable good manufacturing practice (GMP)-compliant manufacturing including validated preservation protocols, and regulatory frameworks accommodating progenitor-stage cell therapies. Together, these advances offer a realistic path toward vision restoration in patients with currently untreatable retinal degenerative diseases.

secondary.title: The Evolving Paradigm of Autism: Folate Receptor Autoimmunity deranging Epigenetic Programming in fetal and postnatal Brain Development.
secondary.abstract: This review on autism provides a summary of the multiple genetic, epigenetic and environmental changes setting the stage for disturbed brain development due to aberrant synaptogenesis and corticogenesis during the prenatal and post-natal periods. The emphasis is placed on nonmendelian transmission driven by epigenetics. Folate deficiency appears to play a critical role in influencing many of the structural changes contributing to developmental deficits. Impaired passage of folate across the placental and the blood-brain barriers to the fetal and postnatal brain because of folate receptor autoantibodies (FRAb) emerges as the major cause. Cerebral folate deficiency with or without autism has been associated with FOLR1 gene defects, a rare disorder. On the other hand, FRAb in association with low CSF folate is present in most children diagnosed with autism. These autoantibodies are present in more than 1/3 of asymptomatic parents of children with autism or are acquired by the child during the first two years of life. Early detection of FRAb amongst autistic children is necessary to enable high dose folinic acid treatment. The use of folinic acid before conception and during pregnancy among mothers or both parents with FRAb, represents a promising strategy to reduce the risk of autism in future offspring. Interventational treatments in parents prior to pregnancy and optimal therapeutic approaches in infants are needed to prevent disordered development of the pre- or post-natal brain.

secondary.title: Axonemal dynein gene dysfunction as a cause of male infertility: insights from DNAH family mutations.
secondary.abstract: Male infertility is a complex disorder and defective sperm motility is one of the most common reasons for impaired fertility. The dynein axonemal heavy chain (DNAH) gene family encode molecular motors that form the structure of cilia and sperm flagella. Abnormalities in several DNAH genes have already been confirmed to be causative factors responsible for male infertility conditions, mainly including asthenozoospermia, multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF), and reproductive failure related to primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD). Here, this review illustrates the current evidence regarding the involvement of members of the DNAH family in male infertility, along with summarizing their biological functions, genotypic and phenotypic correlations and clinical significance. Due to the breakthroughs of the technologies of whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing along with research with animal models and functional investigations, the diversity of reported causative DNAH mutations and their implications for the organization and function of sperm axonemes are currently better understood. DNAH1, DNAH8 and DNAH17 are the DNAH genes most frequently described as being involved in male infertility, though growing evidence also indicated that DNAH3, DNAH11, DNAH12 and DNAH14 also contribute to the male reproductive disorders. Implementation of testing DNAH genes into molecular diagnostics enhances the assessment of genes causing severe sperm motility disorders and aids genetic counseling of the affected families. Together with the genomic and functional data, further research will elucidate additional details for disease mechanisms and will bring benefit to more precise diagnosis and treatments of DNAH-associated male infertility.
